speechtext: A considerable lobby has been carried on for that purpose, but we have not yet seriously considered the matter.
Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance) moved the third reading of Bill No. 278 to amend the Special War Revenue Act.

I wish to move in amendment, seconded by the hon. member for Richmond-West Cape Breton (Mr. Macdonald):
That all the words in the motion after "that" he struck out and the following substituted therefor:
Special War Revenue Act

"In the opinion of this house the application of the sales tax in respect of personal clothing and boots and shoes places a heavy and unnecessary burden upon the people of Canada and should be discontinued forthwith."
No extended argument is required to establish the merit and justice of the amendment which I have just submitted to the house. The sales tax was distinctly a war measure. When first adopted in 1919, it could be justified. At that time Canada was just emerging from the world war. For four years this country had given unstintingly of its man power and financial resources in that great struggle. The obligations arising out of the war were colossal in their nature. Under the circumstances, ordinary methods of raising revenue were not sufficient; extraordinary means had to be resorted to, and the sales tax was one such extraordinary method. But to-day the scene has changed; the circumstances are entirely different. The fiscal year under review records abounding revenues and the Minister of Finance was able to tell the house of a surplus of $69,000,000 in national bookkeeping. Eleven years have elapsed since the consummation of peace. To-day our land, and I use that word in its broad economic sense, our labour, our capital, the creative genius of our people, are all alike devoted to the pursuits of peace, and under these entirely differ-*ent circumstances, Mr. Speaker, the sales'tax, which was distinctly a war measure, now lingers superfluous on the stage of national finance and in my judgment should be completely abolished.
But in this amendment I do not ask for its complete abolition, and for this reason: When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) presented his budget to parliament he told us that out of the $69,000,000 of surplus, some $40,000,000 would have to be earmarked to retire maturing obligations. The revenue derived from the sales tax during the last fiscal year totalled $71,000,000, and were I to move at this time for its complete abolition the Minister of Finance might well reply that complete abolition would interfere with plans that he had for the retirement of maturing ' obligations. I have consequently in my amendment limited the abolition of the sales tax to boots and shoes and clothing, a source from which only about $7,000,000 of revenue is derived, and derived from commodities which enter directly into the family budget of the poor people of this country. Whatever argument my hon. friend the Minister of Finance might make against complete abolition of the sales tax at this time, there is no semblance nor shadow of an excuse for not abolishing it in respect to the commodi-
[Mr. Macdougall.l
ties which I have mentioned in my amendment-commodities which as I have said enter directly into the family budget of the poor people of this country.
In the matter of levying taxes and of remitting taxes every government must be guided by some canon of taxation, and what better canon could this or any other government adopt than the canon of human welfare? What more just than where taxes are levied the strongest backs should bear the heaviest burdens and those who are best able to pay should pay the most? In the matter of remitting taxation and giving relief to the taxpayers, what more equitable than that relief should be given first to those people in our country who most urgently need relief. Under the amendment which I have proposed the beneficiaries will be our farmers, our fishermen, our miners, our lumbermen, the artisans and common labourers of Canada. All I ask this house to do is to relieve those classes of our population of a burden of taxation amounting to some $7,000,000. All I ask this house to do is to join with me in attempting to reduce the cost of living of the masses and correspondingly increase their standard of living.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance has presented to parliament a rich man's budget. It is my privilege to-day to move a poor man's amendment to a rich man's budget, and I move that amendment with the confident expectation that it will be given the sympathetic support of every hon. member of this house, irrespective of party, who wishes to bring a little more of comfort and happiness into the homes and a little more of cheer and encouragement into the hearts of the great masses of the people.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The resolution before you, Mr. Speaker, is that the bill be now read a third time. That bill provides for a reduction of taxation amounting to over $20,000,000, and my hon. friend from Inverness (Mr. Macdougall) moves an amendment which I have not before me, but happily we have two years' notice of it because it is exactly the same amendment as moved by my hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) in 1927, hamely, that all the words after the word "that" be struck out and other words substituted.
Now if that means anything it means that the house will reject the reduction of taxation as presented in the budget of $22,000,000 and will not be declaring for a policy such as was presented in the amendment which was moved to the budget by my hon. friend from South Wellington, speaking for the opposition-a

Special War Revenue Act
policy of protection and the safeguarding of industry. When the budget was under discussion the speeches of hon. gentlemen opposite all indicated, not a desire to help the poor man, not a desire to reduce taxation, but a desire to impose indirect taxation because every hon. gentleman opposite will admit that protection is in a measure indirect taxation. To-day we have the issue put straight before us. We have before us to-day an amendment which proposes to reduce direct taxation. The amendment goes still further. It proposes to wipe out altogether the reduction of $22,000,000 in taxation as provided for in the budget and declares for a policy which, after all, is a policy of direct taxation. It is interesting to consider just how the various elements in this house will regard the amendment. I can quite understand that my hon. friends opposite who seek to impose indirect taxation would support a policy of reducing direct taxation, but I cannot see how some parts of the country that favour a policy of direct taxation could support the amendment.
I admit at once that the sales tax is a direct tax. In that regard it is similar to the income tax, which everyone will admit is a direct tax. If anybody has any doubt as to who pays the sales tax as collected by the retail merchants, because in the last analysis it is the retail merchant who collects the sales tax, and if anybody has any doubt as to who pays the income tax, all they have to do is to consult the circulars that are being sent out at this time by the electric power and light companies in the province of Quebec, who say to their customers: If the government would only reduce the income tax, we should be able to reduce to you the cost of light and power. Now if the electric power and light companies in the province of Quebec are right in that contention-I am not going to discuss that for the moment-then I ask this house who pays the income tax which the government imposes upon corporations, great transportation companies, the big life and fire insurance companies and the banks of this country? And, remember, the larger portion of the income tax, which is a direct tax, comes from the corporations. So I submit that the policy of my hon. friends opposite is a policy of increasing indirect taxation, while making a gesture that they are in favour of reducing direct taxation. I said a moment ago that after all it is the consumer who pays this tax.

Special War Revenue Act

1926 my hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), speaking of the sales tax, used these words:
How are we going to get relief from this oppressive taxation? The method I propose is boldly to strike out and do away with the sales tax.
Apparently that speech was brought to the attention of the Retail Merchants Association of Canada. The secretary of the association directed to the Prime Minister this letter, dated December 15, 1926:
To the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, Prime Minister and President of the Council.
Dear Sir,-We would call to your attention the following statement made by the Hon. Mr. Guthrie, leader of the opposition, in his reply to the address from the throne, delivered on Monday, December 13, 1926, and reported on page 25 of Hansard of that date as follows:
Then they quote the passage that I have just cited.
We cannot find any reply in your address to this statement, and as this is a matter which very vitally concerns every retail merchant in Canada, and more particularly the merchant than the manufacturer, we would like to refer to this statement.
The retail merchants ultimately pay the sales tax and not the manufacturer as the manufacturer simply hands the sales tax on to the merchants who are carrying the stock. The manufacturer does not pay the sales tax until the goods have been sold or invoiced to the purchaser.
If there was approximately $90,000,000 collected in sales tax last year, and the average turnover of the class of merchandise by the merchants on which the sales tax has been paid is four times a year, which we believe is very much higher than the average turnover would be found to be, as while groceries are turned from ten to twelve and even a greater number of times per year, clothing and wearing apparel, in most instances, are not turned in excess of three times and some of the other lines of merchandise even less, but even taking the turnover at a maximum of four .times, the merchants must have merchandise in stock to-day on which they have paid a sales tax in advance to the government in excess of $22,500,000.
We do not believe that the government could do away with this amount of revenue in one year, and we are certain that the merchants in Canada could not afford to take this loss, most of the merchants still holding that the gradual reduction of the tax, as set out in the resolution, would be preferable to its total removal at one time.
The Retail Merchants Association of Canada.
Per N. B. Douglas, Secretary-Manager.
That is the point of view of the men in the trade who collect this tax for the government.
I submit to my hon. friends that in presenting this amendment they are doing no kindness to the many retail merchants throughout the country who have already paid this sales tax in part on the goods on their shelves. Just as sure as we are in this chamber, if this amend-
ment is adopted we will again have before us claims similar to those made by the automobile dealers.
I submit to hon. gentlemen that the policy of the government in gradually reducing both debt and taxation is a sound and sane policy. My hon. friends opposite have frequently referred to the position of the finances of the country. We are glad to have it acknowledged from all sides that Canada to-day is in a good financial condition. The mover of this amendment has said that the sales tax was a war measure. True, the war is over, but the war debt has not yet been paid; the country still has obligations to meet in this respect. We are gradually reducing those obligations. We say to parliament frankly, we are budgeting to take care of maturities as they come along. We propose to take care of those maturities from now until 1933. We are budgeting for that purpose, and I submit to hon. gentlemen, and especially to my hon. friends who are in favour of direct taxation, that the country will prefer the policy of the government in gradually reducing taxes to the resolution as presented by my hon. friend, which I am sure he does not expect to carry. All he wants to do is to be able to say that a hard hearted Minister of Finance refused to accept this proposed reduction of taxation. I submit to him that the orderly method of the government in reducing our debts and taxation is more acceptable to the country than the abrupt wiping out of a tax that will create embarrassment to the retail merchants throughout the country.

Mr. A. D. MicRAE (Vancouver North) : Mr. Speaker, I desire to bring to the attention of the country what I believe to be its greatest problem. I refer to immigration and colonization. In order to do this I will move an amendment to the motion to go into supply.

I decided to see the largest operators in this line of clearing in the west, so I visited Didsbury, Alberta, where I saw the Weber Brothers in action. They are no amateurs, having cleared about 6,500 acres in that district, and their experience on such a large acreage extending over several years is very interesting.
We'ber Brothers keep accurate accounts. Their average cost for cutting, piling, burning and breaking somewhat over 6,000 acres is $6.50 per acre. This includes interest on the investment and depreciation, but no profit.

Were they
selected lands?

No, they were the residue
of the lands in that district. When I was there in November they were on their last contract.
Weber's brush cutter cuts on an average 15 acres per day, at an outlay of $2.57 per acre, a trifle less than the experience at Grande Pr. irie, which is perhaps due to their using heavier equipment. They think on the average $3 per acre will include depreciation and upkeep, but not profit. His tractor also breaks 10 acres a day. By deep ploughing, ten or twelve inches, the stumps are successfully ploughed under, and as two crops are taken off before again plowing the land, the refuse largely disappears and there is little further trouble with it.
Weber says that heavier equipment would be advantageous and thinks a 100 horse-power brush cutting outfit would cut 25 acres a day, and do it for less money. Mr. Weber claimed this cleared land is much more productive than the open prairie in his district, which he accounted for by the fact that repeated prairie fires had more or less burnt off the humus. He states he is willing to take on a contract at any time to cut and burn the scrub at $6 per acre and would make good money. This would leave of my estimate of
$12.50 per acre the sum of $6.50 per acre available for the breaking of the land. This I am sure the hon. Minister of Agriculture will agree is the top price for breaking, even in his old fashioned way, with horses.
I do not know if I have made this modern brush cutting operation clear to hon. members. So as to remove uncertainty and more particularly in the hopes of enlightening my hon-friends, the Minister of Immigration and Colonization and the Minister of Agriculture, as to present day methods, I have arranged for an exhibition. With your kind permission, Mr. Speaker, and with the assistance of the Motion Picture Bureau of the Department of Trade and Commerce, I have arranged to give in the railway committee room, at one o'clock next Wednesday, a moving picture of the modern brush cutter and breaking plough in action, followed1 by other pictures of the up-to-date farming appliances in use in the west. These explain how so few men take care of the ever increasing western crop. I hope all hon. members will attend. I have seen the picture and can guarantee that they will find it worth while.
I now direct the attention of hon. members, Mr. Speaker, to the opportunity we have to make a large number of farms immediately available for settlement in the Peace river district.
It would not require any great administrative ability to assemble and equip clearing units, which might be located at several points, in numbers sufficient to clear and make available along the lines I have indicated homes for at least 2,000 new settlers a year. The personnel of these units would in all not exceed 1,000 men. That is the equivalent of the strength of one battalion. During the war Canada maintained in France 100 battalions as a fighting force engaged in the work of destruction. Should we hesitate now, in peace, to maintain the equivalent of one battalion in the work of construction? We can increase this force as desired.
The clearing and breaking equipment required for the work would not exceed the cost of the guns for a single battery. I can seen no reason, Mr. Speaker, why we should not have the courage to tackle this proposition in a large way, particularly as it could be done under my plan without costing the treasury a dollar.
I have promised the hon. Minister of Agriculture that I would show him a way to clear the heavy scrub land, which he says will cost $25 an acre, for very much less than my [DOT]

Immigration Policy-Mr. McRae
mate of $12.50, to which he has taken strong exception. I refer to clearing land by controlled spring fires.
Through the kindness of the Minister of the Interior I have been furnished with a copy of the report, with before and after photographs attached, which clearly show the result of the experiment carried on by G. J. Lonergan, under the direction of the Surveyor General in May, 1919. This report is a very illuminating one and I commend it to all hon. members who are interested in the clearing of the great Peace River district in a comparatively few years.
I suggest to the government that, instead of keeping forest rangers fire-guarding useless forest reserves in that district, they put these men at the head of crews to burn sections of the country systematically in the spring, and to occupy themselves during the rest of the year providing fire-guards for the following spring's burning operations, and in protecting the country from fall fires, which are undoubtedly injurious to the Land. This could be made a very much needed opportunity to furnish work for new settlers during certain periods each year when it would not interfere with their farming operations.
The report to the Surveyor General shows thac allowing his men 87.50 per day-certainly sufficient-the cost of fire-guarding and burning a very considerable tract, approximately 6,000 acres, was only 10 cents an acre. The report says this acreage was the average scrub country of the north. This statement is borne out by the photographs. It was the same kind of land that the Minister of Agriculture was talking about last year. Lonergan estimated the cost of clearing before burning at $25 per acre. After the fire he estimated the cost of clearing what remained at $5.25 per acre -a reduction of 80 per cent. So by the expenditure of 10 cents an acre a saving of nearly $20 an acre was effected in the cost of clearing this heavy scrub land. The report shows clearly that this spring burning did not damage the soil in the slightest.
This report was endorsed by the officials of the Alberta government-of which the Minister of the Interior was then premier and who, it is said, had great faith in it-as well as by every member of the crew. This included a practical farmer, a resident of the district for about 40 years. Clearing by controlled spring fires is said to have been first advocated by the Association of Dominion Land Surveyors. The report in question was submitted to their annual meeting in 1920, and, I am informed, met with general approval.

The spring fires are possible in the Peace River district as the great growth of grass of the previous year easily carries a hot fire early in the spring before the frost is out of the ground. With two or three burnings at the most, open prairie country results.
I made careful inquiry into this matter during my sojourn in the Peace River country last fall. Of the many men I interviewed on the subject, I did not find one who was not enthusiastic about it. Spring burning they all agreed was not injurious to the soil. All claimed it was the only way to clear up the country. This was endorsed by the government inspector at Peace River Crossing, who added that no damage would result from spring burning. I interviewed the United Farmers of Alberta at Fort Vermilion. They said it was the only way to clear the country.
Mr. Robert Jones, superintendent of the experimental farm there, a very conservative man indeed, supported this method of clearing. The Dawson board of trade held it was the only system and that two burnings would clear the district.
Perhaps the man who was most emphatic on the subject was Mr. W. D. Albright, superintendent of the experimental farm at Beaver Lodge, who said that spring burning is the only way; that it did not hurt the soil, that at most only two or three annual fires would be required to clear an area, and that with a systematic, aggressive policy the whole country could be cleared in from five to ten years.
I am sure the hon. member for Peace River, whom I visited last fall just as he was completing the clearing of a tract of land in the old-fashioned way, will agree with my statement that the proper way to clear the Peace River country is by controlled spring fires.
The cost under this plan would be very much less than my estimate for clearing with mechanical equipment, but the results would not be so immediate. Mechanical equipment should be depended on to provide for the first few years, then systematic spring burning. Beginning to prepare for it this fall would clear the land as fast as required, thus relieving us from most of that part of our expenditure. In a few years at most, open prairie, country fire cleared, would be available to take care of all our incoming settlers.
Once the country is opened up the so-called muskegs which, with an odd exception, are merely the alluvial soil of the country in depressions, covered with moss, will soon disappear and such land will be equal to the best in the district.

Immigration Policy-Mr. McRae
An opportunity to develop an area capable of supporting two million people, thus repeating the western development early in this century, is available to the government with sufficient courage to carry it out.
I proposed last year that the government issue land bonds against their expenditure on such a development. I gave as the maximum required 1300,000,000 for a ten year program, an average of $30,000,000 per year. The hon. Minister of Agriculture in referring to my program, made reference to the loss in the soldier settlement scheme. Buying improved farms at top prices bears no resemblance whatever to partly developing what is undoubtedly better land at no cost for the land to begin with. The soldiers would indeed have been fortunate if some such scheme had been adopted in their case. The history of farm land values is always the same. In good dis-[DOT] tricts, as settlement intensifies, prices move upward. It is the settler who gives the value to the land. This is emphasized by the sale of school lands by the province of Alberta in the Peace river district last year.
On July 16t.h last 36 pieces of raw school lands were sold in the Waterfiole district by auction at an average price of S20.61 per acre, the highest price being $30 per acre.
At Berwyn, north of the Peace river, 50 pieces brought an average of $20.26 with the highest price $40 per acre. The hon. member for Peace River told me last fall that in his district private lands eleven miles from the railway had been sold as high as $25 per acre.
What gives these unimproved lands such values? The answer is-settlement, neighbours. We may expect even better results in the consolidated settlements I am proposing, especially with the improvements I suggest we make on the land.
When the settlement of a district is complete, a land value of $30 an acre would 'be in keeping with the present Peace River values. This means that the homesteader who gets a partially improved homestead for the amount spent on it by the government (which I estimated last year not to exceed $1,500) would not 'be long in seeing that at $30 per acre for his 160 acre homestead he would have a prospective value of $4,800, on which he would owe the government only $1,500. Such a substantial equity in his farm, particularly if, as in the case of the ordinary homesteads, a five-year residence is required, would be a great incentive for the new settler to stick it out, and few homesteaders would abandon their claims and lose their equity 78594-174
by moving into town; and anyway in that event others would be anxious to immediately take their place.
Under my proposal the government would be expending on the land about one-third of its value when surrounded by settlers. Reasonably administered, it should not be possible for the government to lose money in this work. Mortgages on improved farms for about half their value have constituted for years the safest security available on this continent and the experience of the government should not be different from the record of our great mortgage companies, who have made a specialty of farm loans.
It is probable that the maximum advance I have mentioned, namely $300,000,000, will never be reached, as repayments would probably assume proportions which would take care of advances long before the end of the ten-year period. I base this assumption on the fact that our federal government in the early colonization of Manitoba advanced $100,000 to the Mennonites, which was repaid in full with 6 per cent interest within six or seven years. There is no reason why the repayments of advances under this plan should not result in a revolving credit which could be continued indefinitely.
The opening up of Peace River district is a sound national development, even without any fixed settlement scheme. In undertaking it, there need be no worry about farmers to occupy the homesteads when semi-improved. In any event, preference must be given to our own people and more particularly to Canadians. We must look after our own boys first. Making available desirable farms, such as Peace River can offer, will do much to keep our Canadian boys on the farm and will offer them a real inducement to stay in Canada. Not a few labour men in the cities through the country, as a result of my discussion last year, have written me that they would welcome such an opportunity to get back to the land on a farm of their own.
Colonization is the major task before the government. 1 do not believe it can be delegated to a committee or commission with any hope of success. If for no other reason, the doors of approach to government officials at home or abroad would be barred against such a committee or commission. It would have no status abroad and is certain to be abused at home and probably would not be supported even by the government that created it. No, Mr. Speaker, this is the major problem before the country-the first and greatest responsibility of the government today. It cannot be sidestepped.

speakeroldname: Hon. ROBERT FORKE (Minister of Immigration and Colonization):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to speak at any great length and I hope to finish by six o'clock. Although I had some intimation that an amendment would be moved when the motion was made to go into supply on Immigration, I had no idea as to what line that amendment would take. One of the peculiarities of the Department of Immigration is that you have no idea from what quarter an attack is likely to come, it may come from one direction or it may come from another. You may be accused of flooding the country with immigrants or you may be charged with failing to obtain enough immigrants; so I was entirely at a loss to know just what the amendment would be. I was quite relieved when I heard the speech on the amendment, and I want to pay to the hon. member for North Vancouver (Mr. McRae) the compliment of saying that he always has something to offer; it is not a negative amendment, it has a plan and a scheme. Probably it is a product of the imagination; I am sure I could sit down and work out a very nice scheme under ideal conditions, dot the country with fine homesteads and have prosperous and happy people everywhere. It would make very nice reading and perhaps I would get on the front pages of the newspapers and they might say that I had some imagination and some foresight.
I have had forty years of pioneer life and I know something of the conditions which govern the success or failure of these people. I have no fault to find with the proposition which has been offered by the hon. member for North Vancouver and I do not intend at this time to criticize at any length the plan which he has put before the house. I do not believe that any government scheme involving the expenditure of many millions of dollars will in the end turn out to be successful.
In regard to immigration, as I said before, I have observed the people who succeed and the people who fail. I think the people who live on the prairies will bear me out when I say that quite a large percentage of those who started with open prairie under very favourable circumstances have failed and the duty of the Immigration department in connection with any scheme that is brought forward is to see that the immigrant has at ieast a fair chance of succeeding by not being loaded up with too heavy an overhead charge to commence with. I will repeat: I have more faith in the man succeeding who begins slowly as many of our immigrants have done. They have gone up into the northern part of the prairie provinces; they have built themselves log shanties where they have placed
their wives and children, and they have gone out and worked by the day or by the month to earn a little money to start with. Then they have gone back to their homesteads; they have cleared them, and I can tell hon. members that those people, starting with practically nothing, in four or five years find themselves comfortably situated and with good homes. This is being and can be done if you have people who will buckle to and face the difficulties which they are likely to meet.
As regards the trip into the Peace River district, let me say this because I think the hon. member for North Vancouver thought I had lost heart right there at Taylor's Flats and that that was the reason why I had not gone up to Fort St. John. The real truth or the matter is that there was a tremendous downpour of rain and, excepting in the city of Winnipeg thirty or forty years ago, I had never encountered such slippery mud anywhere as on the banks of the Peace river. 1 walked two miles-
And went back three.

That is the old schoolboy
Story we used to tell when we were late. The automobile in which I was riding refused to take the slope and I walked two miles down into the flats, expecting to meet the Hudson's Bay boat there at the river. When we arrived there, it was raining very hard and no boat was to be seen. There was no shelter but the woods where I spent the entire night while it rained heavily most of the time. Next morning a small boat came forty miles up the river and I went in that small open boat, on a very cold morning with heavy rain still falling and my spirits not at the highest, though I did not lose heart.
Mr. MiA'NION: I am afraid my hon. friend is a temperance man getting lost in the woods at night.	[DOT]

When I reached the beat
about six o'clock in the morning I received a very hearty reception from the captain, and the first thing he did was to fetch a bottle of whiskey, put it on the table and say, "That will put you all right."
Did it?

It was the temptation o
my life.
Say whenl

I am very proud to be able to say that I withstood the temptation, got a good, hot cup of coffee and felt as well as one or two other gentlemen who applied the spirits.

Immigration Policy-Mr. Forke

The hon. member did
not climb the hill?

No, I slipped over the hill. I saw a good many hundred miles of the Peace River district although I admit it was mostly in the settled portions. I have nothing but praise for what I saw. It was a revelation to me and I think I will repeat what I said in my speech on the budget, namely, that I was surprised to see the fields of waving wheat ripening in the sun at least ten days earlier than in the older parts of the prairie provinces. I suppose most of that ripening wheat was reaped before the frost did very much damage. The difficulty that [ saw regarding the Peace River country was that of clearing the scrub and small trees which were growing on land that could be made available for homesteads. Of course a large portion of the country is covered with pretty heavy timber and it will take a great deal of work to clear it although something can be realized on the timber. I am quite in accord with what the hon. member for North Vancouver has said as to what can be done with steam power and ploughs in ploughing up scrub. I was very much surprised at the size of the trees that could be pulled down by one of those great ploughs with a strong motor pulling it, but at the same time I think $10 to $12 an acre is possibly too small an estimate for clearing the land.
It would take a good deal of time to analyse all the propositions that have been laid before the house by the hon. member for North Vancouver. He spoke about settling people in a close community and how many families you could place on so many square miles. Human nature being what it is, one cannot control these things as one would like to. He stated that the Department of immigration had allowed people to go into the Peace River district miles and miles away from the railway; in fact he said that was encouraged by the Department of Immigration. That is the Only statement t-o which I am going to object. The Department of Immigration does not encourage people to go any distance away from a railway. I have always contended that no one can carry on successfully more than fifteen or twenty miles from a railway and I have never advised immigrants to go far away from one. I know people have been crossing the Peace river and going as far north as Fort Vermilion almost 100 miles or perhaps more from a railway. I am not very sure of the distances. There is no doubt that this is a

mistake, but they are doing it and what can you do about it? They are free people: they can do as they like. They have the spirit of adventure and if they are making a mistake, they will find it out in the future. But that is what they do, and no department of immigration will prevent their doing it. The same thing occurred on the prairies; when good land could be secured near a railway, you would find people going twenty or thirty miles away just to find the piece of land they wanted at that particular time. The same thing will happen again and you cannot prevent people from doing this.
As regards immigration from the United Kingdom, that was mentioned by the hon. member for North Vancouver, that has been one of the difficulties during this year. We have been continually criticized on account of the lack of British immigrants. The fact of the matter is that there is no difficulty in getting all the British people we want of a certain type if the country could absorb and take care of them. It has been the duty of the department to see that so far as possible the supply of immigrants is not larger than the country can absorb. That is perhaps a little different from the criticism we hear ail the time, that we cannot get immigrants for the Dominion. I would not be afraid to flood this country with hundreds of thousands of people if we want to open the doors and allow all to come who really want to come, but the difficulty is to get the type of people we want who, we know, will succeed and do well for themselves and the Dominion.
Why the difficulty?

Because those people are
not used to go on the land and suffer the hardships and the pioneering work necessary in commencing a new life in a new country. If we can work satisfactorily with the British government, no more of these people wiil come than we think can properly be taken care of, so that no idle people will be walking the streets and seeking employment if the department can possibly help it.
I want to say a few words in regard to the statistics quoted by my hon. friend from North Vancouver (Mr. McRae). He seemed to think that I had made a mistake. I used the figures in a little different way from what he did, but my figures are just as correct as his and hon. members can draw their own inferences. I have had some statistics made up in just a little different way. When immigrants enter this country they are entered by race as well as by country and I tried to

Immigration Policy-Mr. Forke
ascertain how the 166,722 immigrants who came to Canada last year were made up according to race. The figures are as follows:
Racial origin	Number
British		75,581
Northwestern	European	 41,059
All others	 51,082
It will be noticed that the British and northwestern European nations made up 116,640. This constitutes two-thirds of all the immigration that came to Canada last year. Some of these immigrants of the British race may have come from the United States or elsewhere than the British Isles, but they were all British people.
In the calendar year 1928, 54,709 people left Great Britain for Canada; 33,689 for Australia and New Zealand; 7,095 for South Africa; 13,489 for India and other parts of the empire, and 22,345 for the United States. More people came to Canada from Great Britain than to all the other dominions put together, and 32,364 more people came from Great Britain to Canada than to the United States.
Do the figures the minister has given include the harvesters brought out last year?

No. We do not include in any immigration figures more than the 2,000 harvesters who did not go back.
I would also point out that 78 per cent of Canada's population was born in Canada, 12 per cent in Great Britain, and 10 per cent in foreign countries. Surely in view of those figures there is no need for any great alarm on the part of those who are afraid that Canada is going to cease to be largely British and French in its population. I am not saying that to belittle in any way those immigrants who have come to Canada from other countries, because I believe that some day we are going to have a Canadian nationality that will conserve all that is brightest and best in British institutions, and perhaps those immigrants who are coming to our shores from other than British countries will be able to contribute something to our nationality.
The statistics of the department show that we have received 30,560 immigrants from the United States and 33,793 returning Canadians who made declarations that they intended to make their permanent home in Canada. That makes a total of 64,353. The figures I have from Washington of Canadians going to the United States is 57,330, showing a balance in favour of Canada of 7,023. I have some doubts in regard to this figure from Washington because I have seen it stated that the number was 70,000. As the house may know,
we have no records in the Immigration department of Canadians who left for the United States, and we have to trust to the Bureau of Statistics in Washington, which is not always correct. It is difficult to get a correct figure of the number of Canadians who are leaving Canada. My hon. friend from Fort William quoted a figure around 73,000.
I have the figures here of the American authorities, and they show that last year 72,616 Canadians went to the United States.
Those figures were compiled at the border, and they are just as liable to be wrong as right.
That is true of both sides of the line.

It is not a correct figure, but we will let it go at that.
I should like to give the figures for 1924. Our immigration from all sources in that year was 148,560, but instead of 73,000 Canadians leaving this country for the United States, 159,058 Canadians left this country for the United States in that year. So surely the tide has turned and things are very much better than they were just a few years ago.
There is one point of view that I should like to put before the house in regard to the colonization of western Canada, which the hon. member for North Vancouver has brougn* up in his address to-day. It is a fallacy to suppose that the western provinces were colonized by the immigrants who came to this country. Most people seem to think that the great flow of immigrants to Canada colonized the western prairies. I know exactly what took place in Manitoba because I was there. Who can ever forget the long trains loaded with horses and cattle and implements coming from east of the great lakes and colonizing that western country? These were Canadian people. No doubt there was quite a sprinkling of British people too, and there was a colony of Mennonites which has done well, but in the main that western country was colonized by Canadian people from Ontario and the maritime provinces. It was not the 'big immigration that came to this country that colonized Manitoba; I know that. There was at that time a large immigration of foreign people into Canada; a great deal of railway building was going on and public works of all kinds were being undertaken, and these people did that labouring work. They came mostly from Europe; a large part of the money they earned was

Immigration Policy-Mr. Forke
sent back to Europe, and when the era of railway construction ended these people returned to their own countries. That large immigration, therefore, was not at all the benefit that some people really think it was. It was a benefit in the sense that these people by their labour performed a service for the country, but it was not an immigration that was of permanent benefit to the country as a whole.	.
We are told that immigra tion is the supreme need of this Dominion. The whole argument of the hon. member for North Vancouver was that Canada needs a tremendously large immigration. I am not going to say that we do not need immigration; indeed, I should not be true to the position I occupy if I suggested such a thing. But there is this to be considered: will the population that is at present living in Canada gain 'by a tremendously increased immigration? Does anyone here think we shall all be wealthier and happier if we have a population of twenty millions instead of nine and a half millions? That is the thought I wish to suggest. Not that I am condemning the development of the country, but a large immigration does not necessarily mean that we shall be happier or more prosperous. Why has Canada come back so soon after the war compared with other countries that were engaged in it? Because we are a country of nine and a half million people, endowed with great natural resources, and we had something wonderful to fall back on. That is why Canada, with its sparse population and great natural resources, has recovered more rapidly than any other country.
Now, I am afraid I shall be quoted in the newspapers to-morrow morning as condemning immigration. I say we do not want immigration that we cannot take care of; we do not want immigration that will be a burden on the country. We do not want to bring here discontented people who will be unhappy in this country. We want people to come here who will enjoy our prosperity and who will themselves be prosperous. That has been the aim of the department since I have been at the head of it.
Statistics prove that the lack of immigrants has not been the trouble. Last year we absorbed 166,000 immigrants-and our population is only nine and half million. I am going to repeat what I said in my speech on the budget, that we are trying to absorb more people per capita than the United States ever attempted to absorb. When they absorbed 850,000 immigrants their population was at least 100,000,000. Unless you have

some tremendous scheme such as that proposed by the hon. member for North Vancouver, I claim that 166,000 immigrants is no small number for a population of nine and half million to absorb and take care of without dislocating the whole economic system of the country. In the five years from 1910 to 1914 Canada attempted to absorb 1,761,425 immigrants. What happened? Canada suffered from indigestion, and a very small percentage of those people remained with us at the end of ten years. As I said before, the big era of railway building and expansion came to an end, and thereupon those immigrants left the country. It does not do the country any good for this to happen. It may help the transportation companies to bring in hundreds of thousands of immigrants, but when those immigrants do not stay in the country it damages our reputation.
In the past few years great changes have taken place. The wealthiest country in the world, the United States, is facing an unemployment problem. This is one of the paradoxes of modern time-a country the wealthiest in the world and enjoying unprecedented prosperity, and yet with a million and a quarter of its people unemployed. An hon. member speaking some little time ago complained that during the last twenty years this country has been standing still. Well, twenty years ago we were producing 100,000,000 bushels of wheat; last year, with practically the same population, we produced 500,000,000 bushels. That is the economic situation that we have to face. It is so easy to be critical in speaking of this question. It is when you are face to face with the situation that you realize the tremendous difficulties that must be overcome. To-day we have fewer hands engaged in industry, yet there is increase in production. This has brought about unemployment. In the United States the farm population has decreased five and a half million in twenty years. Canadians do not go to the United States to farm. Notwithstanding the great increase in urban population in the United States-and I want the house to pay attention to this-the United States farmer still exports as large a percentage of his produce as he did twenty years ago. He is still dependent upon the foreign market for the price of his goods. I hope those farmers across the line who think they are going to be helped by more protection will realize the fact that they are exporting just as large a percentage of their produce as they were twenty years ago, and that the price they will get for it will be the price which it brings on the foreign market.

Immigration Policy-Mr. Forke
There need be no anxiety for the future of this Dominion. We are the happiest and most prosperous people in the whole world at the present moment. Why all this criticism and discontent as if things were not satisfactory?
You are speaking only for the government.
I am speaking for every individual in Canada.
No.

I know there are no happier people anywhere than in this Dominion, no people who have better reason to be happy. I am not speaking from the political point of view. I am simply stating a fact, and I am sure anyone who considers the situation will admit it to be the fact. There need be no anxiety, I say, for the future of Canada. Development is taking place in all directions. Our business people are holding their own in industry, and we are exporting more per capita than any ether country in the world. Why this despondency? The railways are prospering, reaching out into new districts and providing railway facilities for those people who were venturesome enough to settle in remote districts. In a word, optimism and hopefulness are abroad in the land. Immigrants will come to Canada, Mr. Speaker, I have an idea that in the not far distant future we shall have to take measures somewhat similar to those adopted by the United States to restrict the number of newcomers to the point where we can absorb them.
When we get a new government that might be.

I think you might call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Since the house rose at six
o'clock I happened to pick up the report of the oversea settlement committee in Great Britain, and I came across a few sentences which I shall read, because I fancy they will afford an answer to those who are under the impression that the British people do not appreciate the difficulty of getting their own population to migrate.
In their report for the year 1927 the settlement oversea committee enumerated some of the chief causes, partly political and partly economic, which prevent the more rapid distribution of population as between this country
and the dominions, and particularly of those for whom state aid, o-r at any rate employment on arrival overseas, is essential. Chief among these are:
A. (In Great Britain)
1.	The industrial habits and the townward bent of the general population and its consequent unwillingness, and, without training, unfitness, to take advantage of openings overseas (such openings as concern men, are for the most part in land work, and, for women in domestic work).
2.	The upward tendency of the standard of living and comfort in Great Britain during the present generation.

The Britisher may go at any time within four months of sailing to be examined. He does not need to break up his home or make any arrangements for sailing before being examined. If he passes the examination he is given a medical card which is valid for four months. He does not pay a cent for the medical examination whether it is done by Canadian doctors or by roster doctors. All this expense is borne by the government.
On the continent we have medical officers at Paris, Antwerp, Rotterdam, Hamburg, Danzig and Riga. Medical examination of continental immigrants is conducted only at these ports. The continental immigrant cannot go to a doctor in his own country before sailing and obtain the Canadian medical examination. He can get it only at the port of sailing. He must go to the port some days before sailing takes place in order to give plenty of time for the examination. The difference in the medical examination itself certainly does not favour the continental. If British migrants had to go through the same form of medical examination as central Europeans go through at the ports of sailing, I can assure you that we would have very little British
immigration. If the continental immigrants are not fit they are returned, so that if the immigrant has sold his place and has paid his fare for himself and his family to these ports, and then is found medically unfit, he can be turned right back at these ports.

relatives who are admitted on the ground of relationship apart altogether from the question of occupation:	wives and unmarried
children, and parents and1 unmarried brothers and sisters, of immigrants legally domiciled in Canada who are in a position to receive and care for their relatives.

Immigration Policy-Mr. Glen
There are certain things that should be asked of those who are dealing with the immigration question. In view of the agitation that took place in this country during the last j'ear since the immigration committee sat, I think a statement should be made in this house as to what is being done and as to what we actually want in the matter of immigration.
I would ask what interests are most concerned with and clamouring for an open door policy in immigration? The answer is that most of the criticisms of any policy of restriction in any direction come directly or indirectly from interests which profit by the transport of immigrants.
What provinces are urging more immigration? The answer is, not one of the provinces is asking for more general immigration. I differ entirely from the hon. member for Fort WTilliam when he says that this whole country is asking for immigration; for I am satisfied that I speak for the three western provinces when I say that not a single organization there, except those who profit by the transportation of the immigrants, is asking for more immigrants. I know that some other hon. members will be able to corroborate what I say. It is an absolute fact that in the three prairie provinces there is no demand for immigrants except those who can come into this country with capital and, after landing, can maintain themselves.
Now, thirdly, if the labour situation in Canada is not being fairly met there will be an evident shortage of: (a) farm labour; (b) skilled and other industrial labour; (c) general unskilled labour. Is it true that an unhealthy shortage actually exists?
No.

The answer is that it is not
true. At the beginning of the present month. May, 1929, reports from western Canadla showed a surplus of labour in almost every centre of the west. At Prince Albert continental immigrants were offering to work as general labourers at $1 per day and board themselves.
It is not reasonable to expect that immigration should provide ample labour for the peak of the seasonal demand such as occurs annually in August and September, nor is it fair to hold that immigration should be reduced so as to prevent any unemployment at the other end of the scale during midwinter when seasonal labour is not in demand. It is necessary to avoid either of these extremes.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I submit that we recognize that Canada requires increased

population. But no one will deny that in this stage of our development the governing factor shall be quality and not quantity. I think our department recognizes this factor in insisting upon the examinations, mental and physical, and, if you will, moral, which have been in practice for some time.
The efforts of the department to stimulate and primarily encourage British immigration into this British dominion, the house and the country will support. But with immigration there must of necessity fee given instruction, care and assistance in the period of colonization, and, as I said at the outset, this work cannot be better performed than by the provinces and their units, the municipalities.
These are general principles, but I am satisfied of this, Mr. Speaker. Nothing has been said so far in the debate in condemnation of the policy of the Minister of Immigration during the past year. He has followed up entirely the recommendations made by the committee on immigration which sat last session, with one exception, the granting of homeseekers' fares from eastern to western Canada. I understand from the Passengers' Association that they did not think it was proper to make this concession. I think he has administered his department admirably, and he and his officials are entitled to a considerable amount of credit. I believe that but for the cry for purely British as against any other immigration we would have no amendment offered at the present time. Therefore I wish to give to the minister that meed of praise to which I think he is entitled for carrying out the recommendations of the immigration committee. I believe that the sound, sane policy pursued by the department to-day will be found to be the best for Canada in the long run.

There is, Mr. Speaker, probably no question of a political nature that requires greater thought than this question of immigration. If we are going to carry on a policy of immigration, some valid reason should be given to the country. Yet I think there is no question so badly neglected by social workers, by statesmen and by the public generally than this great question.
To-day seemingly the government follows a policy which has been outlined by the directors of industries in our cities whose chief aim seems to be to direct great waves of human beings to this country for the sake of cheap labour, with the idea of exploiting their capabilities for labour and low living standards so that urban industry may be the better carried on.

Immigration Policy-Mr. Evans
Now, the material or monetary value of a multitude of human beings is perhaps the lowest conception we can have of the value of our immigrants. It is the very lowest conception of a movement on which we are spending millions of dollars each year to bring in people from Europe, the United States, and other parts of the world. Immigration is a failure as far as the increase in the values of land go, if that is the policy we have in mind. It might be a factor in increasing mass production in our cities, that is if mass production depends on the export of goods and the exploitation of the immigrants' ability to live on low wages, coupled with the fact that to-day all our export trade is carried on because the home consumer is paying prices for all manufactured goods that insures a profit over the whole output.
Agriculture can no longer carry the burden of urban industry, but that seems to be the reason to-day for the advocacy of a vigorous immigration policy. If that is what we are doing, then I say we are piling up wrath against the day of wrath, because artificiality in trade sooner or later must be reckoned with. To-day the United States government is face to face with the result of its own policy. The concentration of wealth has gone forward in that country with such acceleration as to render necessary direct aid to their millions of farmers. I want to warn our government that through a false, fiscal policy we have brought about an unstable condition in the industry of agriculture in Canada. That is, urban industry is fast destroying agricultural industries, and also it is destroying community life in our rural areas.
But to return again to land values. If that was the idea of immigration, I want to say it is the development of a community life which increases the value of land. I do not think we can afford lightly to pass over the facts as they face us to-day. First, let us be sure what is the purpose of this nation in spending many millions of dollars to bring in millions of human beings, whom, I am sure, under present conditions it will be impossible for us to absorb in our social and economic life, under our present fiscal system. It is a thorough insight into actual facts and forces with recognition of their bearing upon what makes life worth living that constitutes the true foundation of national life. Woodrow Wilson, not long before he died, said:
All this country needs,-
Speaking of the United States.
-is a new and sincere thought in politics coherently and distinctly uttered by men who are sure of their ground.
President Wilson was conscious that something was wrong, that something was needed in the national life of the United States to offset the selfish attitude of those who at that time not only completely controlled industry and credit-and credit particularly to the agriculturist-but controlled the government of the United States as well. Let me say that practically speaking Canadian urban industry has been built up on the same sort of selfishness, which is ruining the agricultural life of the country to-day and making necessary a policy of immigration. It is destructive of rural life because it drives the virile and what should be the contented farmer, or the farmer's sons and daughters, into the city. If we are going to carry on an active immigration policy for the one purpose of filling our vacant lands, then let us do first things first; and the first thing to do is to find out that farming can be carried on in such a way as to justify our placing on the land an immigrant with the average capital and ability which immigrants have. Those of us in this house who know most about farming can come to only one conclusion on this whole matter:	You cannot make farming pay to-day, either in eastern or in western Canada, unless it is carried on on a large scale. The farmer who is going to be successful in Canada must now be a real capitalist himself. This is why I say that to bring in working people to make homes on the land is a useless policy for the government to pursue; all it can do is to provide cheap labour for urban industry. These industries are controlled by a class of people who admit that they cannot live except by class privilege. They must therefore live by exploiting their workers and the rest of the population. Through high prices this policy has made it impossible to carry on and to compete in world's markets. But the farmer has to compete against the cheap labour of the whole world, and were agriculture to-day to be treated as other industries are treated, if it were possible to do so, you could not keep people off the land wherever there was a farm to be got. It is because of our false economic and fiscal policy that immigration proves to be so futile.
I come now to another point which is bound to create some concern and which the government is bound to take note of sooner or later if our immigrants are to be settled on the land to any great extent by educational and financial aid. I want to ask:	What
is to be done with the product? Will the government of this country have to undertake to guarantee a price in the market for agricultural produce if raised in much greater quantities than it is to-day? That has already

Will the government, let. me ask, take the produce then from the farmer's hands at a profit and treat the agriculturist as we are now treating the capitalist, ensuring a dividend to all expended capital each year?
