All our urban industries are waterlogged, and we give to the capitalist and the industrialist the privilege of fleecing the consumer to pay dividends on this watered stock.
There would be no need of an immigration policy to-day if the agriculturist were treated as he ought to be and the burden of urban industry .taken off hie back. Now last August -on August 14, 1928-there was a conference in Saskatoon among the United Farmers of Canada and the women's section of that institution, the Canadian Legion, the Saskatoon Trades and Labour Council and the rural municipalities of Saskatchewan, and they were alii unanimous in opposing the present immigrationi policy of this government. They urged in a resolution, passed unanimously there, that the government appoint a commission to inquire into the need or other-

wise of immigration, and that 'the commission report here before any policy of the kind be followed.
I want to deal with one or two things in connection with what the hon. member for Fart William (Mir. Manion) has said. He says that the question is of great importance and, further, that matters are not very satisfactorily carried on; in fact, he says that the government's policy has been a failure. He says that we have in Canada three and a half millions of square miles filled with natural resources which need to be developed. Yet he himself has repeatedly, even this session, advocated a policy that fleeces every inhabitant in that great area to provide a living for those who choose to live in a very small area in Quebec and Ontario and who admittedly must have special privilege before they can exist, not having the initiative to go into these great areas where these natural resources are to be found and to develop them and this -country, as the hon. member advocates.
Then the hon. member said we could take many more people of all kinds, and I was glad to hear him make that statement. In answer I want to say that what Canada needs most is a group of business men who will invest capital in industry without first linking up with the politicians as the one essential to going into business in Canada. We want a group of business men who can carry on by their own industry and ability without coming here to seek a special privilege which places an unjust burden upon the whole population. I was glad to hear the hon. member for Fort William put forth that argument.
The hon. member doubted the statement of the Minister of Immigration with regard to prosperity. I want to say that if the wealth in Canada to-day were properly distributed we all would be able to feel something of the prosperity which is said to be prevalent throughout the country. However, the class for which the hon. member speaks does not care to develop the natural resources of this country with their own earnings; they prefer to invest their money in foreign countries. Today we have invested in foreign countries over $1,700,000,000 of Canadian money, the earnings of our agriculturists and others, taken out of their pockets by high prices and high rates of interest, yet those who are concentrating our wealth in the hands of the few do not see fit to put their money back into the development of their own country. That is why we need a policy of immigration; that is why our people are leaving the land, and for one I wish to protest to-night against an immigra-

Immigration Policy-Mr. Maloney
tion policy under which the government brings in peasants from central Europe to take our places when, under present conditions, we cannot live on the land. These are facts we must face, and I want this house to face them squarely.
The hon. member spoke about sheep raising; he said there were twenty-six million sheep in Great Britain, and the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. McLean) interjected that those sheep were raised in that small area without protection. The hon. member for Fort William replied that this was the case because England is the greatest cloth-producing country in the world. Why is that so? Why cannot Canada be, in proportion, an equally great cloth-producing country? The reason is that our false fiscal policy has driven the cost of manufacturing cloth entirely out of line with world prices and we are unable to compete in the markets of the world except by placing the burden upon the agriculturists and workers of this country. Our policy of trade penalties has so driven the cost of production out of line with world prices that we cannot compete in world markets. The labourer and the mechanic, through proper organization, to some extent have raised their wages to meet the high cost of living, but that is something the agriculturist cannot do; he must accept world prices. We have an object lesson today in the United States, where the farmers are calling for direct aid; and what about our own maritime provinces? Even they need direct aid to-day; they cannot live without such aid. Why is that necessary? It is necessary because the cost of manufacture and distribution is such that those who are now producing the greatest part of the national income, the agriculturists, fail to stay on the land and make their permanent homes there.
Again, the hon. member said he wants to keep our young people in our own country, but in my opinion before we can do that we must keep our own money here to develop our natural resources. You cannot take the money out of the pockets of the agriculturists through high prices and high rates of interest and invest it in foreign countries, and at the same time expect our young men to remain in Canada. Of those who have claimed for many years to have a monopoly of patriotism I would ask if they consider it a patriotic act to invest over $1,700,000,000 of Canadian money in foreign countries and then bring in from southern Europe immigrants who are accustomed to a lower standard of living and who work for lower wages. Is that reasonable? We must face first things first; let
those who advocate a policy of immigration be consistent in what they say and do.
The hon. member for Fort William also said that cheap countries are poor countries. Canada is not a cheap country, but I venture to say that the average worker in Canada to-day is no better off than the average worker in any other country, particularly countries such as Denmark and Holland. The United States is not a cheap country; it is not a country of low prices. We have been advised by every advocate of protection in this house to follow the policy of the United States, but to-day the farmers of that country are at their wits' end; they are at the end of their tether and thej can go no further until aid is given. Presi dent Hoover was elected on his promise a agricultural aid.
I merely desired to place some of these ideas before the house, particularly since the hon. member for Fort William did the same thing in a very passionate speech. I want to warn this house that a vigorous immigration policy is not suited to Canada at present. We have plenty of farmers and we appear to have plenty of workers, and unless the government will face this question of finding markets and finding work for all immigrants I think we should be very careful of the class and quantity of people we bring to this country.

I should like to say a few words in connection with this very important matter, but before doing so I might mention that I was very much struck by the speech of the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Glen). In that connection I might report a rumour which I am sure will bring joy to the heart of the Minister of Immigration and at the same time consternation to the hearts of many hon. gentlemen from the western provinces who for some years have stood solidly behind the government. The rumour is that my hon. friend the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke) is about to be raised to the dignity of a senatorship and that his successor in the cabinet as Minister of Immigration will be the hon. member for Marquette.
Either of them would be good.

If that is the intention of the government, I do not think the selection will secure for this country an adequate supply of immigrants, and that is very unfortunate indeed. After hearing the hon. member for Marquette I was struck bv the fact that you

Immigration Policy-Mr. Maloney
could not tell whether he favoured bringing immigrants into the country or keeping them out. There is one thing I will say for him, he was honest in many of his declarations. He stated that in various sections of western Canada there were men who were willing and ready to work for a dollar a day and board themselves. If that is the fact, can that be considered as a strong advertisement to induce the outsider to come here and seek a home in Canada? What a sad commentary on the efficiency of the present government!
The question of immigration has been dormant throughout this present session; nothing has been heard of it until to-day. This seems all the more significant in view of the fact that last session it was perhaps the most important of all topics discussed by the house. It was a topic which engaged the attention of a very important committee of members of the House of Commons, men who sat day after day, week after week, taking evidence from every part of the country. They had before them men of science, men of everyday walks of life, men who are at the head of our great industrial organizations and transportation systems. They all told their story and it was all taken down. Their evidence was aimed at the one point, that increased immigration would be the salvation of this country. What has become of the labours of that committee? All this evidence has been pigeon-holed and carefully hidden away in some obscure government office, resting side by side with many other abortions which may be laid at the door of the present government. What a sad disappointment it is to those people of Canada who had the high hope, after hearing of the extensive investigations of that committee, that this question of immigration was about to be definitely settled for all time to come. What a disappointment there must be in the hearts of the people of Canada when they consider the attitude of the government in connection with that matter.
How different is the attitude of the hon. member for North Vancouver (Mr. McRae). He brings forth a bold, advanced scheme, remembering as he does that we in this country have stupendous resources as well as staggering liabilities. The hon. member realizes that we require men and women of the right type to assist us in developing and exploiting those resources but who will be willing to share the liabilities with us. Realizing that fact, the hon. member presented a bold and advanced plan for the colonizing of this country. Right at this point I beg to extend to him my very sincere congratulations on the

magnificent- effort which he put forth this afternoon. He spoke because of personal contacts; he depicted the possibilities of that section as perhaps few members of this house would be able to do. He had confidence in his argument, and I for one see much of merit in what he had to say because I believe his project would solve many of the difficulties now confronting the people of Canada in the matter not only of provision for future immigrants but also of providing occupations for those who are now here.
I believe that people of the right type, no matter where they come from, are the most desirable for Canada at the present time. There is one phase which strikes me more forcibly than any other in connection with the problem of immigration, and that is the bringing back to this country of those of our sons and daughters who are to-day living outside of Canada and earning a living away from home. The most important aspect of the whole immigration question is that which has to do with the repatriation of our fellow Canadians who are now living in the United States. Our population to-day is estimated at about 9,500,000. Consider the fact that at least half as many more are residing outside of Canada; almost 5,000,000 Canadian people are to-day living in the United States. That is a very pathetic condition. Our every effort should be bent in endeavouring to recover those who have gone from our shores, but up to the present we see no evidence of any improvement so far as that phase of the question is concerned. It is true that the Minister of Immigration quoted figures; it is true that he haggled for two or three minutes on the figures of some 25,000 Americans who had come here and some 30,000 Canadians who had returned. They came back, but for a visit only. More than half of those he mentioned stayed here for two or three weeks with the old people at home and then returned to the United States with a brother or sister for whom they had procured employment. During the last seven years we have lost 240,000 more than our total immigration for the same period. During that period 962,000 immigrants entered Canada; in other words, we lost 1,200,000 people in the last seven years. Where did they go to? In looking over a monograph issued by the Department of Commerce of the United States I find that French-Cana-dians comprise 33.1 per cent of the foreign-born white population of the state of Maine; they comprise 42 per cent of the foreign-born white population of the state of New Hampshire; and they comprise 31.8 per cent of the foreign-born white population of the state

Immigration Policy-Mr. Maloney
of Vermont. The French-Canadians are our greatest colonizers, and we have allowed them to escape from Canada, their native home, to settle in a foreign land. Why should that be? These men and women should be back here in Canada and to that end our every effort should be bent. The same thing applies to Canadians who are not of French extraction. That class of Canadians comprise 35.9 per cent of the foreign-born white population of the state of Maine, 15.3 per cent of the foreign-bom white population of the state of New Hampshire, and 24 per cent of the foreign-born white population of the state of Vermont. Take the totals: Canadians as a whole comprise 69 per cent of the foreign-born white population of the state of Maine, 57.3 per cent of the foreign-born white population of the state of New Hampshire, and 55.8 per cent of the foreign-born white population of the state of Vermont.
If we go farther west we find that the border states from New York right through to the Pacific coast are filled with our sons and daughters. That is a pathetic situation. Why should it exist? It has been said here to-day, and it has been said before, that the attraction of the larger for the smaller body may have something to do with the situation. In other words, the force of gravity comes into operation, but for the benefit of those who reason in that way I would say that there is another physical law, another physical force greater even in its application, its might, than is the great force of gravity. I refer to the force of cohesion, that force which binds and holds together the various units of any body. The Canadians who are now in the United States are bound, to us by that power of cohesion. They cherish the land of their birth; the years of their childhood days are ever before them. They are our own flesh, blood and bone; why should we not make every effort to have them return?
It is said that population depends greatly on subsistence; that wherever we have the most food suitable for sustaining the human race, there we find the greatest congregations of people. It is said that the people in those sections are happy in proportion to the quantity of food which a day's labour will procure. If that be a correct statement, why should Canada not be filled from end to end with the very best type of citizens selected from all over the world? Here we have a country independent economically of the rest of the whole, wide world; no other country on the face of the earth is more independent economically than is the great Dominion of Canada. We can, if we so desire, live within 78394-176
ourselves for all time; we do not have to depend for our existence on any other nation, and yet when the Hawley-Smoot proposals were laid before the congress of the United States a short time ago, the comments made thereon by some of our citizens were somewhat perturbing. We had for example our good Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell), when he heard the news of what the proposals meant to the people of Canada, reported by the newspapers as shouting: "Good cheer, we shall survive." Of course we shall survive. We shall survive in spite of the Hawley-Smoot proposals. We shall survive in spite of the inaction of the government in the matter. Let me say that the worm will turn some day; the farmer of Canada who is to-day the under-dog will, just as soon as there is a change of government in this country, come into the position which is his, namely, a position of prosperity. The minister must feel that, -had our friends to the south gone further and imposed a little extra tariff in addition to that which they have proposed, the}r would have crushed us out of existence; that we are dependent on them almost completely. Has it come to this, that a country situated and endowed as ours is to feel that it is dependent on any foreign power? Has it come to this, that we, free men of Canada, are compelled to turn the other cheek and say to those of our competitors who see fit to impose trade barriers against us: If you do not increase the tariff too greatly, we shall survive. Such an attitude of mind on the part of our statesmen is sufficient to make any Canadian's red blood boil. I submit that is a condition which should be remedied by the government of this country.
The United States of America had their immigration problem just as we have ours. In 1810 the population of the United States was 8,000,000. In 1812 a war which broke out forced that nation to fall back on their own resources and to manufacture that which they needed for themselves. The result was a tremendous advance in industry in that country, and with that advance and growth of industry there occurred an accompanying development and opening up of new lands. It is a positive fact that during almost three-quarters of the last century the United States of America absorbed more than 30,000,000 unassisted immigrants, men, women and children. Why? Because the immigrants followed prosperity; with the industrial and agricultural development which took place after the war of 1812, the trend of immigration could not be stopped. The resuit was that in a comparatively brief period more than 30,000,000 people came into that country

unassisted. There is in this a very striking lesson for our own country. The population of Canada to-day compares wiith that of the United States of a century ago. We have in our possession to-day resources which perhaps they did not have in those days, resources which are superior in many respects to those possessed by the United States. We must do what the United States did after the war of 1812, namely, manufacture our own raw products in our own country and import raw materials to manufacture for our own use as required instead of exporting to the United States and other foreign countries hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of raw or semi-raw products to be manufactured abroad, bringing work, comfort and happiness to men and women of a foreign nation rather than our own. Let us manufacture these products at home: let us give that work to the boys and girls of this country; let us increase our population as the United States did theirs after 1812, and then Canada will not require any government assistance in regard to immigration. If conditions such as these were brought about, among the first to return to Canada would be many of the 5,000,000 Canadians who are to-day south of the line, men and women who can never forget the old home ties, who are looking longingly to Canada, their home, awaiting an opportunity to come back and better themselves.
This government has never made an honest effort to aid immigration; in fact, on the other hand, it has apparently done what it could, without too much publicity about it, to impede immigration. The Minister of Immigration and his prospective successor spoke in the house this afternoon and evening, and yet we cannot honestly say whether they are prepared to receive immigration or whether they are anxious to keep it out. They are marking time. That is not what we desire in Canada. As a matter of fact, the whole history of this government has been against bringing immigrants to Canada. I notice in the Hansard of March 20, 1923, a statement quoted that was made by the Minister of the Interior. He said:
What is the use of bringing people to this country if they cannot exist?
That was a fine advertisement for this great Dominion of Canada, coming from the lips of an important member of the government. If he held those views in 1923, they must of necessity be greatly accentuated at the present time because conditions in Canada to-day are less favourable for the ordinary individual than they were in 1923. Take agriculture, for instance. The position of the farmer in this country is not an enviable one.

Let me read a short extract from a speech delivered by Captain John D. Cameron, of the Canadian Pacific Railway colonization department. Speaking a few weeks ago in this city he said:
He had recently surveyed old Ontario and he was amazed to find rural figures in many places now stood lower than they did before confederation. The rural population of Oxford county was 40.969 before confederation, and now was only 23,342.
That is in Oxford county, the garden of the great province of Ontario. If the farming population of the ooutnity of Oxford has become depleted to that extent, surely the government should take heed and do something to remedy the conditions. What has the government done to encourage the farmer? What has it done to encourage the young men and the young women to stay on the farm? What has it done to make farming more profitable and more pleasant? Has it done a solitary thing to aid the farmers? It did do one thing. By order in council, passed without the sanction of parliament and without the consent of the people, the government entered into an agreement with New Zealand under which thirty million pounds of New Zealand butter were brought in last year, thousands of tons of beef and lamb, and at the same time millions and millions of dozens of eggs were allowed to come in from the United States and China, all of which were thrown on the open markets of this country to come into competition with the produce of the Canadian farmer. Is it any wonder that the rural population of the great county of Oxford has become rapidly depleted, as shown by the statement of Captain Cameron? The farmer who works from early [DOT]morning till late at night will, I am sure, appreciate the fact that the government has allowed one of his competitors seven thousand miles away from here to ship in his produce almost free of duty-the very products that the Canadian farmer is endeavouring to supply.
If the scheme proposed by my hon. friend for North Vancouver should go into effect it would relieve the situation to a considerable extent. It would, in the first place, apply to our Canadians, something which no scheme brought forward by this government up to the present time has done. It would give the farmer and the farmer's sons in eastern Canada and in western Canada the right to take advantage of the privileges which this scheme offers. It would give to our Canadian boys in the United States who are to-day anxious to get home an opportunity to return and start life on the farm in this great western

Immigration Policy-Mr. Rowe
country. It would relieve the unemployment situation to a great extent. It would repatriate many of our citizens. It would bring happiness to a great many of the citizens of this country.
If we want immigration we must improve conditions. We must make Canada a country fit to live in, a country which will attract the better elements from all over the world. To do that we must have a complete change of front on the part of our government.
In the first place, to be prosperous and happy and to attract immigrants to our shores, we must manufacture our raw materials at home. We must bring in raw materials to manufacture for our own purposes where required. We must preserve the home market for our farmers; we must preserve the home market for our industrialists. We must make Canada the greatest producing nation on earth, and when we have accomplished that let us see to it that markets are found throughout the length and breadth of the world. When these conditions are brought about Canada will have no need of a minister of immigration and no need of an immigration policy, for immigration will flow to us, unsolicited, from all sides.

Mr. Speaker, in view of the constructive suggestions that have been offered from this side of the house and the criticism that has been made of the Department of Immigration, I feel that I must confine my observations to a very limited time.
Probably one of the most fundamental problems affecting the growth of a young country is that which relates to immigration. The keen interest that the Canadian people have taken in this great problem is indicated by the comment and continued criticism 'of the public press, the churches, societies of various kinds, organized business interests- not the least among which have been the two great transportation systems in Canada-as well as criticism by the opposition party which sits to your left, Mr. Speaker, in this house. We have indeed a real problem on our hands. Lack of interest in it has been shown by the inactivity, dire neglect, and stagnant attitude of the present administration. Since they came into power they have talked of unbounded prosperity. They have received proposals of assistance from the British government, which has set aside $225,000,000 to assist the emigration of the unemployed in Great Britain to the British dominions. During all these years the government of Canada has been jostling about this Department of Immigration, letting 78594-1761
it grow daily weaker and weaker like an illegitimate child crying for adoption. In 1922, when this government came into power, immigration and colonization was thrown into the Department of the Interior, under the careful management of the present Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart). In 1924-25, the department for a while was taken care of by the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb). Afterwards it was taken care of for a time by the Hon. Mr. Low, and later, in 1925, just prior to the election, it was loaned for a time to the Hon. Mr. Gordon, the then member for West Peterborough, afterwards sadly defeated in that riding. In 1926 it was again thrown into a corner of the Department of the Interior, under the tender care of the present Minister of the Interior. In 1926, when this great ship of state set out to sea, the department was used as a political lifebuoy to pick up the then drifting captain of the Progressive boat. We find that he had with him in these stormy waters the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) as first mate.

I have no doubt that his friends on this side of the house who followed him so loyally through those years will be satisfied with his declaration that he no longer wishes to bear their name.
While, Mr. Speaker, we have had no lack of schemes proposed in the immigration department, those schemes have never been put into execution. Since this government came into power we have had eight speeches from the throne enunciating six different policies on immigration; in two years there was no policy set forth. In 1922 the speech from the throne contained this pronouncement: We must have a renewal of effort on the part of the Immigration department in order to bring in an increased number of immigrants. In 1923 the speech from the throne contained this statement: We must have a wide expansion, a new publicity program, a program to reach throughout the empire and also into the United States and other foreign countries. In 1924 there were two or three changes of ministers and no policy. In 1925 the speech from the throne contained another pronouncement on immigration. In that year we on this side of the house recall the manufacture of that famous phrase "The high cost cf living". It *was discovered that the only relief for this condition was greater production, and that the only way to bring this about was to increase the flow of immigration. Therefore the government decided that efforts must be made to increase immigration to bring about that greater production', and incidentally to extend the settlement of crown lands, with special consideration of the Peace River district. In 1926 the speech from the throne stated that in view of the favourable conditions prevailing in the Dominion the government had formed a new and comprehensive immigration, policy, and as a eorolliary the government proposed a broad repatriation scheme by way of rural credits 'and other benefits to the country districts'. In 1927, although six new ministers had been appointed since 1921, the then holder of the portfolio started the year without any policy at all. But in 1928 another new policy was announced. The speech from the throne stated: We must have cooperation 
with the different provinces, we must pass the responsibility on to the provincial authorities, and we are now going to make a definite attempt to bring in British youths under a special settlement scheme. In the speech from the throne this session, in pursuance of the recommendations of the committee on immigration and colonization, we were to enter into an arrangement with the different provinces to bring to Canada juvenile immigrants who were to be strictly selected for their adaptability as settlers with a view to promoting general prosperity throughout the Dominion.
Now, after all this publicity, after six years with programs announced and two years without any at all, we find the Minister of Immigration still drifting peacefully on the quiet waters of government inactivity. Today we realize that the government of Canada has practically no immigration policy. It is not much wonder that through all this confusion we have the present stagnation in immigration. Illuminating figures have been placed on Hansard to-night. Everyone throughout the Dominion realizes that the flow of immigration has been changed almost to a flow of emigration; tens of thousands of our best sons and daughters have left their native land for the United States. I venture to say that in the New England states to-day there are almost as many French Canadians as there are, Mr. Speaker, in your native province. We have heard supporters of the government state to-night that they do not want any more immigration. They are prepared to concede that Canada needs a few more of the right class, a few "hand-picked" immigrants. I submit that while they are handpicking those immigrants the department will have no time for any other activities. In fact the real work of the department will stagnate as usual.
